title: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies
outcomes: Explain the meaning of deposit and identify amounts excluded from it.
Distinguish depositors, eligible companies and exempt companies.
Apply the procedure and limits for deposits from members and from the public.
Explain trustee, tenure, interest and procedural rules.
Explain the remedies and punishments for default.

meta.exam_tip: Exclusions come with conditions — always state the condition (60+15 days, annual salary, 365 days, 5 years, ₹25 lakh single tranche).

concepts.title: Meaning of deposit and amounts excluded
body: Section 2(31): "deposit" covers any money received by a company by way of deposit, loan or in any other form, except categories prescribed in consultation with the RBI. The definition is inclusive, so the label used does not matter.

Many receipts are excluded (see table). If excluded advances for goods, property or capital goods become refundable because the company lacks the required approval, they become deposits 15 days after falling due for refund.
Deposits may be secured (fully, by a charge on tangible assets) or unsecured. A partly secured deposit is treated as unsecured and must be described so in every circular and advertisement.
concepts.analogy: A company borrowing from the public is treated like a bank in miniature, so the law looks at substance, not names.
concepts.work: An employee required to keep a ₹7 lakh interest-free security deposit on a ₹6 lakh salary has made a deposit.

head: Not a deposit (examples)
Condition
rows: From Government, local or statutory authority; guaranteed by Government
Loans from banks, PFIs, insurance companies; from another company
Allotted within 60 days or refunded within the next 15 days
From a director (or, for a private company, a director's relative)
Written declaration that it is not borrowed money; disclosed in Board's report
Secured bonds/debentures (first or pari passu charge on non-intangible assets); bonds compulsorily convertible within 10 years; listed unsecured NCDs
Secured amount ≤ market value of assets
Trade advances for goods or services
Period within business practice or 5 years, whichever is less
Promoters' unsecured loan required by a lender
Only until the bank or FI loan is repaid
₹25 lakh or more in a single tranche from one person
blocks.title: Rule 2(1)(c) exclusions

concepts.title: Depositor, eligible company and exempt companies
body: Depositor: a member who deposits under section 73(2), or any person who deposits with a public company under section 76.

Eligible company: a public company with net worth of at least ₹100 crore or turnover of at least ₹500 crore that has passed a special resolution and filed it with the Registrar before inviting public deposits. Within the borrowing limits of section 180(1)(c), an ordinary resolution is enough.

Banking companies, NBFCs, housing finance companies registered with the NHB and other notified companies are outside these provisions. The deposit rules therefore govern non-financial companies such as manufacturers and traders.
A private company can accept deposits only from its members. A public company that is not eligible can also accept only from its members.
concepts.analogy: Only big, approved public companies can knock on the general public's door.
concepts.work: A public company with turnover of ₹420 crore and net worth of ₹80 crore may borrow only from its members.

concepts.title: Deposits from members (s. 73) and exemptions for private companies
body: Section 73(2): a company accepting deposits from members must pass a resolution in general meeting; issue a circular in Form DPT-1 to members showing financial position, credit rating, number of depositors and dues; file it with the Registrar 30 days before issue; keep at least 20% of deposits maturing in the next year in a deposit repayment reserve account in a scheduled bank by 30 April; and certify that there has been no default in repaying deposits (or, if there was, that five years have passed since it was made good).
The circular is valid until the earlier of six months after the close of the financial year or the date of the AGM (or its last due date); a fresh one is needed each year.

Private companies are exempt from the circular, filing, reserve and certification steps if they accept from members up to 100% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium; or are start-ups for five years from incorporation; or are not associate or subsidiary companies, have borrowings below twice paid-up capital or ₹50 crore (whichever is lower) and are not in default. They still file details in DPT-3.
concepts.analogy: Even borrowing from your own members needs transparency and a repayment cushion.
concepts.work: A 3-year-old private start-up taking money from its members skips the DPT-1 circular but files DPT-3.

concepts.title: Deposits from the public by eligible companies (s. 76)
body: Section 76: an eligible company may also accept deposits from the public, applying sections 73 and 74 with necessary changes.

It must obtain a credit rating each year from an approved agency (at least investment grade) and state it in the invitation; publish its DPT-1 circular as a newspaper advertisement, in English and in the regional language, (and its website), filed with the Registrar at least 30 days earlier.
Secured deposits need a charge on tangible assets (not intangibles) within 30 days, worth at least the deposits and interest, valued by a registered valuer, in favour of a trustee for depositors.
Limits: from members 10% and from others 25% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium; an eligible Government company 35% overall.
concepts.analogy: Public money comes with ratings, advertisements and a trustee watching.
concepts.work: An eligible company offering secured deposits must create the charge within 30 days of acceptance.

concepts.title: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules
body: Tenure: not repayable on demand or within six months, and not longer than 36 months. Up to 10% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium may be raised for short-term needs if repayable after at least three months.
A company that is not eligible may accept up to 35% of that base from members; private companies up to 100%, and start-ups (10 years) and some small private companies without limit.

Trustee for depositors: written consent, deposit trust deed in DPT-2 at least seven days before the circular, and independence from the company. Removal before the term ends needs consent of all directors present at a Board meeting, with an independent director present where required. The trustee calls a depositors' meeting on requisition by one-tenth in value, or on a default.

Other rules: interest and brokerage within RBI limits for NBFCs; brokerage only to authorised agents; depositor's declaration that the money is not borrowed; up to three joint holders; nomination; deposit receipt within 21 days; register kept for eight years; DPT-3 return by 30 June; penal interest of 18% p.a. on overdue claimed deposits; terms cannot be changed to the depositor's disadvantage.
Premature repayment after six months: interest at 1% below the rate for the period actually run (a part year of six months or more counts as a full year; less is ignored).
concepts.analogy: Six months to 36 months, 21 days for the receipt, 18% if you are late.
concepts.work: A deposit of 1 year 5 months is treated as 1 year for the premature repayment rate.

concepts.title: Default, Tribunal remedy and punishment (ss. 73(4), 74, 76A)
body: Section 73(4): if a company fails to repay a deposit or interest, the depositor may apply to the Tribunal for payment and compensation for loss.

Section 74: deposits accepted before 1 April 2014 that remained unpaid had to be reported to the Registrar within 3 months and repaid within three years or by maturity, whichever was earlier; the Tribunal may allow more time on the company's application. Default attracts a fine of ₹1 crore to ₹10 crore for the company and, for officers, imprisonment up to 7 years or fine of ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore, or both.

Section 76A: for accepting deposits in breach of sections 73 or 76, or failing to repay on time, the company pays the deposit and interest and a fine of at least ₹1 crore or twice the deposit (whichever is lower), up to ₹10 crore. Every officer in default faces imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine of ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore; a wilful breach intended to deceive attracts section 447.
Breach of a rule with no specific punishment: fine up to ₹5,000, plus up to ₹500 for each day a continuing breach lasts.
concepts.analogy: Taking deposits illegally is punished more harshly than most company law breaches.
concepts.work: A company that illegally accepts ₹30 lakh faces a minimum fine of ₹60 lakh, as twice the deposit is lower than ₹1 crore.

illustrations.title: How much can Kaveri borrow?
illustrations.q: Kaveri Ltd., a public company with turnover of ₹640 crore, has paid-up capital ₹40 crore, free reserves ₹60 crore and securities premium ₹20 crore. (a) Is it an eligible company? (b) What are its limits for deposits from members and from others? (c) How much may be repayable in under six months? (d) What would the members' limit be if it were not eligible?

jobs.title: Is this a deposit?
jobs.situation: While auditing a manufacturer, you find advances from customers, a loan from a director's brother and share application money held for five months.
steps: Check whether customer advances were adjusted within 365 days.
Note the company type: a director's relative is excluded only for private companies.
Check allotment within 60 days or refund within 15 more days.
Report deposits in DPT-3 and the CARO comment.
jobs.takeaway: Test each receipt against the specific exclusion and its condition.

jobs.title: Planning a deposit scheme
jobs.situation: A public company with net worth of ₹150 crore plans to raise public deposits.
steps: Pass and file the special resolution.
Obtain credit rating and appoint a trustee with DPT-2.
File the DPT-1 advertisement 30 days before publication.
Fund the 20% repayment reserve by 30 April.
jobs.takeaway: Sequence matters: approvals and filings come before the advertisement.

mcqs.q: Share application money becomes a deposit if allotment is not made within 60 days and it is not refunded within:
mcqs.explain: Application money is excluded only while it is appropriated against allotment. If securities are not allotted within 60 days and the money is not refunded within the next 15 days, it becomes a deposit. Adjusting it for another purpose is not a refund. In practice: diarise both dates.
mcqs.topic: Meaning of deposit and amounts excluded

mcqs.q: An employee's non-interest-bearing security deposit is excluded from deposits only if it does not exceed:
mcqs.explain: The rules exclude a non-interest-bearing security deposit taken from an employee under the contract of employment only up to the employee's annual salary. Anything larger is treated as a deposit. In practice: compare with current salary.
mcqs.topic: Meaning of deposit and amounts excluded

mcqs.q: Money received by a public company from a director's relative is:
options: Not a deposit if a declaration is given
mcqs.explain: The exclusion covers money from a director of any company, but money from a director's relative is excluded only for a private company. For a public company it is a deposit. In practice: check who actually paid the money.
mcqs.topic: Meaning of deposit and amounts excluded

mcqs.q: A public company is an eligible company if it has net worth of at least:
options: ₹100 crore or turnover of at least ₹500 crore
mcqs.explain: Rule 2(1)(e) defines an eligible company as a public company with net worth of not less than ₹100 crore or turnover of not less than ₹500 crore that has the required shareholders' approval filed with the Registrar. In practice: either test is enough.
mcqs.topic: Depositor, eligible company and exempt companies

mcqs.q: Which company is NOT governed by the deposit provisions of the Companies Act?
mcqs.explain: Banking companies, NBFCs, NHB-registered housing finance companies and notified companies are excluded, because other regulators govern them. The rules target non-financial companies such as manufacturers and traders. In practice: check the RBI registration.
mcqs.topic: Depositor, eligible company and exempt companies

mcqs.q: The deposit repayment reserve account must hold, by 30 April each year, at least:
options: 20% of deposits maturing in the following financial year
mcqs.explain: Section 73(2)(c) requires at least 20% of deposits maturing in the next financial year to be kept in a separate scheduled bank account, used only for repaying deposits, and never allowed to fall below that level. In practice: plan the April cash need.
mcqs.topic: Deposits from members (s. 73) and exemptions for private companies

mcqs.q: A private company is exempt from issuing the DPT-1 circular if it accepts from members not more than:
options: 100% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium
mcqs.explain: Private companies accepting member money within 100% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium are spared the circular, filing, reserve and certification steps, though they still report in DPT-3. Start-ups and some small companies get similar relief. In practice: compute the aggregate first.
mcqs.topic: Deposits from members (s. 73) and exemptions for private companies

mcqs.q: The longest tenure for which a company may accept deposits is:
mcqs.explain: Deposits cannot be repayable on demand or within six months, and cannot be accepted for more than 36 months. Short-term deposits up to 10% of the base may run for three to six months. In practice: set scheme tenures between these limits.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules

mcqs.q: An eligible company may accept deposits from persons other than members up to:
options: 25% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium
mcqs.explain: For eligible companies the rules allow 10% from members and 25% from others, each measured on paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium. An eligible Government company may go up to 35% overall. In practice: track the two limits separately.
mcqs.topic: Deposits from the public by eligible companies (s. 76)

mcqs.q: A deposit receipt must be issued within:
options: 21 days of receiving the money or realising the cheque
mcqs.explain: The rules require a receipt signed by an authorised officer within 21 days from receipt of money, realisation of the cheque or renewal, showing date, name, amount, rate and maturity. In practice: build this into the deposit process.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules

mcqs.q: Penal interest payable on matured deposits claimed but not repaid is:
options: 18% per annum for the overdue period
mcqs.explain: Rule 17 requires a penal rate of 18% per annum for the overdue period on deposits, secured or unsecured, that have matured and been claimed but remain unpaid. This is in addition to the punishment provisions. In practice: repay on time.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules

mcqs.q: A deposit trust deed in Form DPT-2 must be executed:
options: At least 7 days before issuing the circular
mcqs.explain: Where secured deposits are invited, the company must appoint trustees with their written consent and execute the deposit trust deed at least seven days before issuing the circular or advertisement. In practice: the advertisement states the trustee's consent.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules

mcqs.q: A company illegally accepts deposits of ₹40 lakh. The minimum fine on the company under section 76A is:
mcqs.explain: The minimum fine is ₹1 crore or twice the deposit accepted, whichever is lower: twice ₹40 lakh is ₹80 lakh, which is lower than ₹1 crore. The maximum is ₹10 crore, and the deposit with interest must also be repaid. In practice: officers face separate punishment.

mcqs.q: If a company fails to repay a deposit, the depositor can apply to:
mcqs.explain: Section 73(4) lets the depositor apply to the Tribunal for an order directing payment of the sum due and compensation for any loss caused by non-payment. The Tribunal may pass other orders it thinks fit. In practice: keep the deposit receipt and claim letters.

questions.q: Sudha Pvt. Ltd. received ₹12 lakh from the brother of its managing director without any declaration, and ₹8 lakh as customer advance for machines delivered after 14 months. Are these deposits?

model.provision: Rule 2(1)(c)(viii) and (xii)(a), Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014
model.facts: Money from a director's relative of a private company; trade advance adjusted after 14 months.
model.analysis: Money from a director's relative is excluded for a private company only if the relative declares in writing at the time that it is not borrowed money, and the Board's report discloses it. A trade advance is excluded only if adjusted against supply within 365 days, unless the advance is the subject of legal proceedings.
model.conclusion: Without the declaration, ₹12 lakh is a deposit. The ₹8 lakh adjusted after 14 months also becomes a deposit.

remarks: Apply each exclusion with its condition.

summary: Deposit = any receipt by way of deposit, loan or otherwise, less prescribed exclusions.
Eligible company: public, net worth ≥ ₹100 crore or turnover ≥ ₹500 crore, special resolution filed.
Members: resolution, DPT-1 circular filed 30 days earlier, 20% reserve by 30 April, no-default certificate.
Receipt 21 days; register 8 years; DPT-3 by 30 June; penal 18%.
s. 76A: company ₹1 crore or 2× deposit (lower) to ₹10 crore; officers 7 years + ₹25 lakh–₹2 crore.
remember: Director's relative excluded only for private companies.
traps: Eligible company member limit is 10%, not 35%.
Premature rate is 1% below the rate for the period run, not the contracted period.

viva.q: What makes a public company an eligible company?
viva.model: A public company with net worth of at least ₹100 crore or turnover of at least ₹500 crore, which has passed a special resolution and filed it with the Registrar before inviting deposits from the public.

viva.q: What is the deposit repayment reserve account?
viva.model: A separate scheduled bank account in which a company keeps, by 30 April each year, at least 20% of deposits maturing in the next financial year, to be used only for repaying deposits.

viva.q: What are the tenure limits for deposits?
viva.model: Deposits must be for at least six months and at most 36 months; up to 10% of capital, free reserves and premium may be taken for three to six months for short-term needs.

viva.q: When can a trustee for depositors be removed?
viva.model: Only with the consent of all directors present at a Board meeting, with at least one independent director present where the company must have independent directors.

viva.q: What punishment applies to officers for accepting deposits illegally?
viva.model: Imprisonment up to seven years and a fine of ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore; if the breach was wilful and meant to deceive, action for fraud under section 447.

cases.title: Sunshine Appliances Pvt. Ltd.
cases.case: Sunshine Appliances Pvt. Ltd., incorporated 7 years ago, is a subsidiary of a listed company. Its paid-up capital is ₹5 crore, free reserves ₹3 crore and securities premium ₹2 crore. It wants to accept deposits from its members and from some customers' relatives, offering 6-month and 48-month schemes and a cash gift to whoever brings in depositors.

mcqs.q: Deposits from customers' relatives who are not members are:
options: Not allowed, as a private company may accept deposits only from members
mcqs.explain: A private company can accept deposits only from its members. Only an eligible public company can take deposits from the public. In practice: the scheme must be restricted to members.
mcqs.topic: Depositor, eligible company and exempt companies

mcqs.q: Maximum member deposits Sunshine may accept:
mcqs.explain: A private company may accept from members up to 100% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium: ₹5 + 3 + 2 = ₹10 crore. Being a subsidiary, it does not get the unlimited relief for small companies. In practice: report in DPT-3.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules

options: Not permitted, as tenure cannot exceed 36 months
mcqs.explain: The rules cap the tenure of any deposit at 36 months; a 48-month deposit cannot be accepted or renewed. The 6-month scheme is within limits. In practice: redesign to 36 months or less.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules

mcqs.q: The cash gift to people who bring in depositors is:
options: Brokerage allowed only to persons authorised in writing who actually procure deposits, within RBI limits
mcqs.explain: Brokerage may be paid only to a person authorised in writing to solicit deposits and through whom deposits are actually procured, within the rates prescribed for NBFCs. Gifts to anyone else breach the rules. In practice: appoint authorised agents.
mcqs.topic: Limits, tenure, trustees and procedural rules
